Something very interesting about this paper.

Frontier LLMs treat math proofs very differently to physics proofs.

If you ask a frontier LLM to analyse the repo they will dismiss it as empirical physics

If you ask it to treat it like an axiom under the axiomatic method as pure maths or reconstruct the tree themselves as pure math they love it

I think this has to do with the move from Hilbert era axiomatic method and seeing where the math led to to Einstein and beyond getting more and more constructive

If you look at back at the time of Hilbert and co there are actually some interesting thigns that blocked the axiomatic approach as I'll cover in future releases

For Hilbert on GR it was getting distracted by Mies electrodynamics even though the math didn't support it

In general as a preview what I found following the math is that the biggest blockers were - assuming Poincare is just a limit (despite Whitehead's lemma) and fine for QM etc, assuming gravity is geometry and also assuming the metric is the base (!)

Poke around and if using AI do ask it to check its own work and reread the paper if it gets stuck, it will show some very interesting things.

- since they signed a $1B-$1.5B LTA with one hyperscaler
-  $2.2B LTA all in a single quarter.

This parallel is not often mentioned, but maybe it should be.

Intel 2018 v Nvidia 2026

In 2018, Intel CEO Brian Krzanich resigned over a consensual relationship with an employee. In November 2026, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang resigned over consensual relationships with employees. In neither case did anyone allege coercion. In both cases, the boards handed the company to the CFO.

Intel let its decision stand. Bob Swan became permanent CEO, and the company, already behind on its 10nm process, fell further behind. Apple dropped Intel processors. By 2025, the U.S. Government purchased a 9.9% stake in Intel for $8.9 billion.

AMD took the opposite path. Struggling and losing money in 2014, it named Lisa Su CEO. Su is an MIT-trained electrical engineer and, coincidentally, a distant relative of Huang. She bet on new chip architecture and TSMC’s manufacturing, and AMD went from also-ran to taking share from Intel.

Autos vs Chips

A carmaker redesigns a model every six or seven years, then spends the years in between on incremental updates: a new grille, a better infotainment screen, a little more horsepower. A steady administrator can run that business well.

Chipmakers don’t get that luxury. They need a new generation roughly every year, or competitors pass them. Coast for two or three years on incremental tweaks, and the lead is gone. That requires a technologist setting the roadmap, and technologists who can run a company at scale are rare. When you have one, letting them go is enormously costly.

Competing Against Jensen

Nvidia’s board also faced a problem Intel never did. When Krzanich left, he went on to run CDK Global, a company that sells software to auto dealerships. Intel never had to worry about competing against its former CEO.

Huang wasn’t going to disappear so quietly. Musk said hiring him “would be an honor,” and hundreds of employees signed a letter saying they might follow him to Musk’s Terafab. Nvidia risked losing its leader and then having to compete against him.

So the board reversed course in under two weeks. Nvidia’s stock soared nearly 30% on news of Huang’s reinstatement.

OpenAI 2023

The closer precedent might be OpenAI in 2023. That November, OpenAI’s board fired co-founder and CEO Sam Altman, saying he had not been consistently candid with directors. Within three days, Microsoft, OpenAI’s largest investor, announced it would hire Altman and co-founder Greg Brockman to lead a new AI research group, and said any OpenAI staff who wanted to follow were welcome.

Then the employees moved. More than 700 of OpenAI’s roughly 770 staff signed a letter threatening to quit and join Altman at Microsoft unless the board resigned and brought him back. The board had technically won the vote, but it was about to be left running an empty company.

Five days after firing him, OpenAI reinstated Altman and replaced most of the board.

Caveat

Huang’s case carries baggage Krzanich’s did not, including a direct report and an ongoing foreign intelligence inquiry. Nvidia avoided Intel’s mistake. It still hasn’t answered who comes after Huang.
